blocks.text: A radiotherapy beam at National Hospital Abuja, an X-ray film at a state specialist hospital, and the Nigeria Research Reactor-1 at Sheda all use ionising radiation under strict control. The same three emissions — alpha, beta and gamma — appear in every WAEC radioactivity paper, and the same safety rules (time, distance, shielding) keep staff and patients safe.

blocks.markdown:
**Radioactivity** is the spontaneous, random decay of an unstable nucleus with the emission of radiation. You cannot speed it up or slow it down by heating, crushing or chemically combining the sample: it is a nuclear, not a chemical, process.

Three common emissions:

- **Alpha ($\alpha$)** — a helium nucleus, ${}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}$ (or ${}^{4}_{2}\alpha$), charge $+2e$.
- **Beta ($\beta^{-}$)** — a fast electron, ${}^{0}_{-1}e$, emitted when a neutron in the nucleus converts to a proton.
- **Gamma ($\gamma$)** — a high-energy photon, ${}^{0}_{0}\gamma$. It often follows $\alpha$ or $\beta$ decay as the daughter nucleus sheds leftover energy.

rows: Lowest (stopped by paper or a few cm of air)
Moderate (stopped by a few mm of aluminium)
Highest (reduced by thick lead or concrete)
Deflected more, as a negative particle
blocks.caption: Ionising power and penetrating power run opposite ways: the most ionising radiation (α) is the least penetrating, because it loses energy quickly in collisions.

blocks.title: Balancing nuclear equations
blocks.text: Nucleon number A is conserved; proton number Z is conserved (counting the charge of the emitted particle). α: A falls by 4, Z by 2. β⁻: A unchanged, Z rises by 1. γ: A and Z both unchanged.

blocks.markdown:
Examples:

$$ {}^{238}_{92}\mathrm{U} \rightarrow {}^{234}_{90}\mathrm{Th} + {}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He} $$

$$ {}^{14}_{6}\mathrm{C} \rightarrow {}^{14}_{7}\mathrm{N} + {}^{0}_{-1}e $$

**Background radiation** is the count you get with no source present — cosmic rays, radon from rocks, traces in food and building materials. Always subtract it from a measured count rate before doing half-life arithmetic.

blocks.title: A half-life calculation
blocks.prompt: A radioactive sample has a half-life of 8.0 days. Its mass is 80 g. Calculate the mass of the original nuclide remaining after 24 days.

steps.text: Find how many half-lives fit into 24 days.
After each half-life the remaining amount is halved.
The other 70 g has decayed into daughter nuclides; it has not vanished, but it is no longer the original species.

items: Handle sources with long tongs — increasing distance cuts dose (inverse-square for a small source).
Use shielding matched to the radiation: paper is enough for α, aluminium for β, lead or concrete for γ.
Never point a source at the body; store it in a labelled lead castle; do not eat or drink in the laboratory.
Monitor with a GM tube or film badge, and subtract background when measuring activity.

blocks.title: WAEC and JAMB tip
blocks.text: Count half-lives; do not divide the original amount by the time. After two half-lives one quarter remains, not zero. In equations, β⁻ raises Z by 1 because a neutron has become a proton. And do not say α is 'more dangerous' without specifying: outside the body γ and β penetrate; inside the body an α emitter is the most damaging because it ionises densely.

points: α is a helium nucleus (highly ionising, weakly penetrating); β is an electron (moderate both); γ is a photon (weakly ionising, highly penetrating).
Balance A and Z: α changes A by −4 and Z by −2; β⁻ leaves A unchanged and raises Z by 1; γ changes neither.
Activity (or remaining amount) follows A = A₀ (1/2)^{t/T½}. Subtract background first.
Radioactive decay is spontaneous and random; heat and chemistry do not change the half-life.
Safety: tongs, shielding, short time, large distance, and never point a source at yourself.
